identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Dharmasthala is widely cited as an example of shared Hindu-Jain religious life: the sanctum's Shivalinga, worshipped as Manjunatheshwara, is served by Madhwa Vaishnava priests, while the temple and its charitable institutions are administered hereditarily by a Jain family holding the title Heggade (Dharmadhikari). The town also holds shrines to four Dharma Daiva guardian deities, a marble Jain basadi to the tirthankara Chandraprabha, and a 39-foot Bahubali statue, and is known for providing free meals to every visitor irrespective of faith.

narrative.summaryIntro: Shri Kshetra Dharmasthala is a Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva, worshipped here as Sri Manjunatheshwara, in the town of Dharmasthala on the banks of the Netravati river in Dakshina Kannada district, Karnataka. Temple tradition credits its founding, roughly 800 years ago, to the Jain chieftain Birmanna Pergade, whose descendants — holding the hereditary title Heggade — have administered the institution ever since. The Shivalinga is worshipped by Madhwa Vaishnava priests even as day-to-day administration of the temple and its charitable institutions remains with the Jain Heggade family, a combination widely described as an example of shared Hindu-Jain religious life. The complex also includes shrines to the goddess Ammanavaru and to four Dharma Daiva guardian deities, the marble Chandranatha Basadi dedicated to the Jain tirthankara Chandraprabha, and a 39-foot monolithic statue of Bahubali on a nearby hill. The current Dharmadhikari is Dr. D. Veerendra Heggade, who has held the post since 1968. The temple is known for free communal meals provided to every visitor and for its annual Lakshadeepotsava, when roughly a hundred thousand lamps are lit across the complex.
narrative.documentedHistory: According to the temple's own historical account, Dharmasthala was originally the village of Kuduma in Mallarmadi, where the Jain chieftain Birmanna Pergade and his wife Ammu Ballalthi lived in a house called Nelyadi Beedu. Temple tradition holds that four Dharma Daivas (guardian deities) — Kalarahu, Kalarkai, Kumaraswamy and Kanyakumari — directed the couple to build shrines in their honour; Brahmin priests engaged for the rituals then asked that a Shivalinga also be installed, and the vassal Annappa Swamy is said to have brought the image of Manjunatheshwara from the Kadri Manjunath temple near Mangaluru. Around the sixteenth century the then administrator Devaraja Heggade invited the Dvaita saint Vadiraja Tirtha of Udupi, who declined to accept hospitality until the linga had been consecrated by Vedic rite; after performing the reconsecration himself, he is said to have named the place Dharmasthala, "the abode of dharma." The temple's own history page states that twenty-one generations of the Heggade family (a name derived from Pergade) have since held the hereditary post of Dharmadhikari. In the twentieth century the post passed from Manjayya Heggade (1918-1955) to Ratnavarma Heggade (1955-1968) to the present Dharmadhikari, Dr. D. Veerendra Heggade, who succeeded to the position on 24 October 1968 at the age of nineteen. Since 1973 the temple town has also held a 39-foot monolithic statue of Bahubali on a nearby hillside — though a district government page instead dates it to 1980 — and since 1972 the institution has organised mass weddings for couples who could not otherwise afford one; Wikipedia records that 10,698 couples had married through the programme as of 2013.

visitingInfo.accommodationNotes: The temple trust operates guest houses at Dharmasthala; per the official site, bookings can be made only through www.shridharmasthala.org and not through any other platform.
visitingInfo.nearestRailStation: Puttur Railway Station, about 49 km (Karnataka Tourism); the Dakshina Kannada district government page instead names Mangaluru Railway Station, about 72 km — the two government sources disagree on which is nearest.
visitingInfo.nearestBusStation: Mangaluru Central Bus Stand, about 74 km (Dakshina Kannada district government page); Karnataka Tourism gives no bus distance.
visitingInfo.nearestAirport: Mangaluru International Airport; Karnataka Tourism states 75 km, while the Dakshina Kannada district government page states 82 km.
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Temple helpline 08256-266666, office 08256-266655, fax 08256-277116; trust office hours 9:30 AM-2:00 PM and 4:00 PM-9:00 PM. The temple's own routine page notes that darshan and pooja timings vary on special occasions, so confirm same-day timings locally before travelling.

openingHours.notes: The temple's routine page states the shrine gates open at 4:00 AM; general morning darshan runs 6:30-11:00 AM. The page notes that temple timings may vary on special occasions.
Resumes after the midday Nithyabali procession, per the temple's routine page.
Followed by the evening Mahapooja at 8:30 PM, per the temple's routine page.

shrines.locationDescription: The main sanctum of the temple, housing the Shivalinga which temple tradition holds was brought from the Kadri Manjunath temple near Mangaluru.
Shrine to the goddess Ammanavaru within the temple complex.

shrines.shrineName: Shrines to the Dharma Daivas (Kalarahu, Kalarkai, Kumaraswamy, Kanyakumari)
shrines.deityOrSubject: Kalarahu, Kalarkai, Kumaraswamy and Kanyakumari — guardian deities of the founding legend
shrines.locationDescription: Four shrines that temple tradition holds were built by Birmanna Pergade before the Manjunatheshwara Shivalinga was installed beside them.
A white marble Jain basadi within the Dharmasthala complex, dedicated to the tirthankara Chandraprabha.

A 39-foot monolithic statue of Bahubali on a 13-foot pedestal, carved from a single block of granite, on a hillside near the temple complex. Wikipedia and the Wikimedia Commons file description both give 1973 as the year of installation; the Dakshina Kannada district government page instead states 1980.

poojas.description: Special abhisheka to the Shivalinga; the temple's routine page links its significance to Lord Rama's worship of Shiva in his Rudra form.
Recitation of the thousand names of Shiva.
Principal food offering to the deity, followed by distribution to devotees.
The temple's principal midday worship, with the idol decorated in Vedic ornamentation, hymn recitation and temple instruments.
A processional offering performed three times a day; general darshan is briefly suspended during the rite.
The evening processional offering that closes the day's worship.

Ceremonial weighing of a devotee against offerings. The temple states that this and other special poojas or utsavas require advance booking through the temple's Parupathyagar and cannot be performed on festival days.
poojas.bookingMethod: Contact the temple Parupathyagar in advance.

festivals.gregorianRuleOrDate: November-December; exact dates vary by year
festivals.significance: The temple's major annual festival, when roughly one hundred thousand lamps are lit across the complex. The temple's own website also associates the festival with an interfaith 'All-Faith Conference,' and Karnataka Tourism describes accompanying literary and religious discourses.

festivals.gregorianRuleOrDate: February-March, per the Hindu lunar calendar
festivals.significance: Hindu festival marking the night of Shiva, listed among the festivals observed at the temple.
An annual anniversary observance associated with the Bahubali statue at Dharmasthala; the temple's official website references its 44th edition.

sources.claimScope: Deities worshipped (Manjunatha, Ammanavaru, Chandraprabha, Kalarahu, Kalarkai, Kumaraswamy, Kanyakumari); founding date and founder; the 16th-century reconsecration; the hereditary Heggade/Dharmadhikari administration; festivals including Maha Shivaratri; SDM group institutions.

Its statement of 'nearly 20 generations' of Heggade succession is not perfectly consistent with the temple's own claim of twenty-one generations or with Veerendra Heggade's Wikipedia page, which describes him as 21st in the line; the exact generation count is treated as approximate rather than settled.
